items.title: Mark Lynskey Opens Up About the Tragic Toll Behind the Bankruptcy
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: For the first time, the notoriously private co-founder goes on the record about the string of devastating personal losses that forced the Chattanooga institution to the brink.
items.lbText:
Mark Lynskey is famous for not speaking to the press, but today, that streak comes to an end. Following the April 30th Chapter 11 bankruptcy filing of Lynskey Performance Products, he has gone on record with Bicycle Retailer and Industry News to explain the profound personal losses that brought the storied brand to where it is today.

The Lynskey family has deep, respected roots in American titanium manufacturing. After launching Litespeed in 1986 and selling the brand in 1999, the family made a triumphant return to the industry in 2006 under the Lynskey Performance banner. Operating out of Chattanooga, Tennessee, the company quickly established a highly regarded domestic fabrication facility.

However, Lynskey reveals that the company’s recent unraveling was triggered by a tragic and severe leadership vacuum. Over the last few years, the brand suffered the deaths of plant manager Steve Kirby, head machinist Bill Thompson, veteran welder Louis Scroggins, and eventually, co-founder David Lynskey.

This cascading loss of institutional knowledge devastated management and production. In response, the company pivoted to heavily discounted direct-to-consumer and eBay sales. That shift in turn alienated its established dealer network, compounded existing supply chain gridlock, and ultimately forced the Chapter 11 filing.

Sitting down with Dean Yobbi to discuss the human toll behind the headlines, Lynskey remains focused on the future: “As a family, we are dedicated to bringing this brand back to what it represents.”

To see the numbers behind the reorganization, the company’s current operating status, and its strategy to rebuild dealer trust, read the complete feature at Bicycle Retailer .

items.title: Ultra-Wide and Coming in 29, 30.5, and 32 Sizes: The Newmen Streem G.48 CS
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: Newmen’s newest carbon wheelset pairs a wide 45mm rim with premium aero spokes, and commits to the next generation of gravel geometry with three distinct diameters.
items.lbText:
Today, German wheel brand Newmen has launched the Streem G.48 CS, a carbon wheelset that supersizes the modern gravel rim. If you aren’t familiar with Newmen, the company was founded in 2016 by former Syntace engineers Michi Grätz and Fabian Merz. They hit the market fast, presenting the very first products—the super-lightweight Advanced SL X.22 carbon wheelset and an aluminum sibling, the Evolution SL X.A.25—at the 2016 Eurobike show for the 2017 season. Since then, the brand has become known for designing lightweight, highly engineered cycling components—primarily wheelsets and cockpits. Most recently in the gravel world, though, it’s been ultra-wide wheels.

The latest Newmen Streem G.48 continues that thread with a 48mm deep carbon wheelset the brand positions as a “true all-rounder” covering everything from “after-work rides, bikepacking adventures or the next gravel race.”

As expected, this is a 48mm deep wheel, but what stands out is the width. The wheelset is built around a generous 45mm external width and a 27mm inner width that Newmen states is “perfectly matched to modern gravel tyres.” To manage handling and compliance, the brand uses a “bulbous rim profile” designed to “absorb impacts efficiently” while retaining an “extremely low sensitivity to crosswinds.” The rim uses a hooked tubeless-ready bead and hides the valve inside the rim using an internal aero valve system.

At the top of the range, the Streem G.48 CS model utilizes silver decals and features a claimed weight of 1,390 grams for the set. The CS build is laced with 21 VONOA Aero Wide Carbon spokes front and rear, attached to Newmen’s FADE R CS centerlock hubs. The hubs feature standard 12x100mm and 12x142mm spacing, support XD, Shimano HG, and Microspline freehub bodies, and are rated for 60Nm of max torque. The total max system weight for the wheelset is 130 kg.

All carbon-spoke wheelsets in the lineup are hand-built at the company’s facility in Kempten, Germany, while a forthcoming steel-spoke variant will be hand-built in the Czech Republic. Perhaps the biggest attention grabber in the news, though, is the detail that Newmen plans to offer more wheel sizes. As reported by BikeRadar, 30.5- and 32-inch diameter wheels will be available “in the future.”

Neither version of the Newmen Streem G.48 is currently available. The carbon-spoked version will eventually cost £1,499 and will be available first with the steel-spoked wheelset priced at £1,250 and promised starting in spring 2027. For more information visit the Newmen website .

items.title: A Literal Love Letter to Steel: The Custom Cicli Barco Road Bike
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: This is how you solve modern bike problems in steel when you consider aesthetics as an equal partner with usability.
items.lbText:
When it comes to steel frames, there’s always a story about a legendary frame that was built by someone with no credit. One name on the down tube, but different hands building it. It’s often talked about in hushed whispers—“did you know?” But for the people actually building those frames, it’s an opportunity.

Cicli Barco is a custom steel frame builder in Italy, but it’s also a contract build shop, and the story we heard from Gianluca Barco at Bespoked Osaka was one of pride in that history. The company website tells of “Granda Mario,” who built “handcrafted frames used by legends like Freddy Maertens and Eddy Merckx” without real recognition. Barco spoke with pride, though, saying that the family’s reputation for high-quality fabrication has shifted that dynamic. Today, while Cicli Barco still splits production evenly between a company label and contract work, the Barco name carries such prestige that other brands now proudly advertise when their frames are “made by Barco.”

Under the Cicli Barco label, the brand produces around 100 frames a year, blending traditional craftsmanship with modern design concepts. For Barco, this contract work isn’t just about paying the bills; it provides a valuable avenue to experiment with new techniques and view frame building from different perspectives.

At Bespoked Osaka, Cicli Barco brought a literal “love letter” to this craft. To be clear, that’s literal as in half of the frame is covered with a handwritten “love letter,” creating a stop-in-your-tracks aesthetic. As Barco explained, while anyone can source tubes and parts, developing a unique signature that makes a bike undeniably a “Barco” is one of the hardest achievements for a frame builder.

The true engineering standout on the bike, however, is a zero-stack head tube designed to integrate seamlessly with modern cockpits without resorting to oversized tubing. Instead of a standard straight head tube, Barco uses a modular central section that can be adapted to specific sizes and geometries. The main tubes are spot-welded to this central part, and a special tool is used to shape the tube to fit the headset cup. Once the cup is inserted, the weld is finished and then reinforced with silver brazing, resulting in an incredibly narrow and clean aesthetic.

It’s an elegant solution to a problem that modern metal bikes are plagued with, but the execution is mirrored throughout the rest of the bike. Look at the seatpost clamp, and you’ll see TIG welding and silver brazing used once again to solve a modern bike problem that, once you see it, you can’t unsee. On this bike, there is no collar. Instead, the seat stays have a bolt through them that, when tightened, closes the cut in the seatpost and acts as a clamp without the visual bulk of one. Like the head tube, it’s so genius it has to be highlighted, but it’s not simple. Using both welding techniques together allows the builders to tightly control material deformation, giving them the freedom to explore complex designs without compromising the structural integrity of the steel.

To finish off the build, the parts have to match. Just like the metalwork, there’s a beautiful balance of clean lines, high technology, and functionality. The drivetrain is SRAM RED XPLR AXS with a CeramicSpeed OSPW and an INGRD crank. The handlebars—featuring an integrated stem—and the wheels come from Polymer Workshop, a brand that has also staked its reputation on solving modern integration problems and fitting into as many contemporary frames as possible. In this case, the definition of modern is slightly turned on its head, but aesthetically, everything is a perfect match. The deep wheels bring a contrast of black that matches the handwritten text, the fork, and the INGRD chainring. There are pops of chrome in the RED drivetrain, and there are even easter eggs of red in the script that match the Italian flag at the back of the bike.

items.title: Arguing About the Future of Gravel Bikes
items.author: Will Tracy
items.content: We rode six gravel bikes head to head at the Velo Field Test, so what did we actually learn about the future of gravel?
items.lbText:
Welcome to this special episode of the Velo Podcast from our 2027 Field Test , where we asked one very important question: What does the future of gravel look like? We took six bikes that couldn’t be more different and compared them head to head.

This podcast is part of our 2027 Velo Field Test. All episodes are streaming now!

The all-rounder: race it or go adventuring.

We started our future of gravel exploration on a first impressions loop, then put the six bikes through a series of head to head challenges, and finally took them on a 100km ride with varied terrain up to Whistler, BC.

Now, Levy, Josh, and Logan have some thoughts about what they just experienced and where the future of gravel is headed. items.title: ‘It Definitely Wasn’t Good’: Ineos Vowed the Transition Was Over. 2026 Shows It’s Only Just Starting.
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Netcompany Ineos head of racing Geraint Thomas sees signs of recovery in the former superteam. An exodus of talent will test the momentum in 2027.
items.lbText:
Netcompany Ineos is on the way back to its former glories – still .

Speaking this week on his Watts Occurring podcast, team head of racing Geraint Thomas insisted that 2026 was only the start of the newly financed squad’s quest to regain relevance in the WorldTour.

“It’s all about that progression, and it’s where you’re starting from as well. This might be a headline now, but let’s say we’re at 20 percent of what we used to be, to pick a number. You can’t just go from 20 to 80 straight away,” Thomas told his co-host Luke Rowe.

“It’s like climbing a ladder, isn’t it? It’s the same thing with a team, and I think we’ve gone up the ladder a couple of steps, for sure,” Thomas said. “We slipped a few times as well, but that’s all part of it.”

2026 was promised to be the year for Netcompany Ineos.

Seven years after the last of its seven Tour de Franc e titles, this would be the year of reboot.

Thomas, freshly retired from a career devoted to the team, was bringing his racing nous and good vibes to the directors’ chair.

Former yellow jersey mastermind Dave Brailsford was back pulling the strings.

The mid-season arrival of Danish IT brand Netcompany offered a path back to superteam status with its pledge to invest €100m over five years.

As Thomas said at the start of the year: “There’s been a lot of talk about transition – ‘the team’s in transition, blah blah blah. The transition’s over now, mate.”

UAE Emirates XRG, Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, and Visma Lease a Bike were warned.

Netcompany Ineos learned that transition takes time in an era defined by a small few phenoms.

In 2026, the team finished eighth in the WorldTour rankings, only a squeak ahead of Uno-X Mobility and Soudal Quick-Step.

A total of 36 victories through the season was the team’s best return since 2023, but strip away the filler and it’s not so pretty.

Eight of that haul came from national championships, the bulk were lower-ranked races, and only 13 were from the WorldTour.

That baker’s dozen is only a fraction of what was gobbled by the teams Netcompany Ineos is aspiring to beat. Tadej Pogačar, Isaac del Toro, Jonas Vingegaard, and Matthew Brennan powered UAE and Visma to two and three times that number, respectively.

Looking further forward, Netcompany Ineos’ two marquee wins in 2026 came from a rider who’s on the way out.

After a sensational victory at Dwars door Vlaanderen and the inevitable time trial victory at the Giro d’Italia, Filippo Ganna is leaving for Lidl-Trek this winter. More on him later .

Thomas insisted the results didn’t tell the whole story as he appraised his team’s season on Watts Occurring .

The Welshman highlighted how a myriad of mechanicals and crashes pulled the handbrake on a young team focused on three newly recruited captains.

“I think it’s all learning as well. Even though results weren’t particularly sensational, we had a lot of wins, but they were smaller wins,” he said.

Thomas’ positive spin on the season was well founded.

Oscar Onley, Dorian Godon, and Kévin Vauquelin all came to the team in the winter to fill high-stakes leadership positions.

Godon harvested victories in tough guy sprints. The Frenchman was one of the revelations of the season.

Onley was denied the chance to do what he was signed for – lead the team at the Tour de France – due to injury . But the rising young Scot rebounded for sixth overall and the white jersey at La Vuelta.

Vauquelin managed to get at least something on the board at the Giro d’Abruzzo after he was whacked by sickness in summer and lost time on day 1 of the Tour de France.

It’s good, but it’s not good enough for a former powerhouse that still judges itself against its own past.

Thomas was confident that there were green shoots behind a season of misfortunes and what-ifs.

Thymen Arensman and Egan Bernal put the team into the picture at the Giro d’Italia while its three new leaders began to acclimate to the team.

“People have said, ‘you can say was our season good or bad?’ And purely from results, I’d say it definitely wasn’t good,” Thomas said.

“I feel like Dorian, Oscar, and Kévin are all new to the team. That takes a bit of gelling,” he said. “The fact that they executed is a big plus. I think they all learned. And I think they’ll all take that forward, and it’s part of that growing. They’re all still young.”

The long-promised transition isn’t over. It’s only just starting for a team with a new identity and new leaders.

The question is, can the transition hold momentum into 2027?

Eight months after Netcompany bowled in, and a year after the arrival of Thomas, Onley and Godon, the team is facing more overhaul.

Ganna, one of the team’s biggest stars and a guaranteed source of time trial wins, broke his contract to join Lidl-Trek.

Rising U.S. talents Artem Shmidt, Andrew August, and Magnus Sheffield are all leaving as part of a talent exodus that’s seen eight riders find contracts elsewhere.

Also, the retirement of Ben Swift feels symbolic. The 39-year-old was the one survivor of the original Sky team that once upended and then dominated the sport.

Netcompany Ineos might struggle to fill the void left by so many significant departees in 2027.

After rumor of poaching Paul Seixas flittered out, the wannabe super team followed a moneyball recruitment policy focused on young talents or mid-career journeymen.

Benjamín Noval is the headliner of the nine arrivals confirmed so far, despite him only being 18 years old. Netcompany Ineos saw so much potential in the kid who dominated junior worlds that it reportedly gave him the biggest contract ever for a rider his age.

Speaking at the time, team CEO John Allert said Noval is the team’s future.

“At the heart of our team is a belief in long-term development and investing in the next generation of talent. Benjamín represents that future – and we’re delighted he’s chosen to grow and develop with us,” Allert said.…

items.title: The Traka Goes Global in Major Gravel Racing Shakeup
items.author: ahood
items.content: The new seven-round Traka World Series replaces Gravel Earth, with equal prize money, global events, and plans to livestream every race.
items.lbText:
The Traka World Series is a new format with seven events. (Photo: Gruber Images)

The Traka is taking its flagship brand beyond Girona and putting its stamp on a new gravel racing circuit.

Organizer Klassmark will launch The Traka World Series in 2027 to replace the Gravel Earth Series , officials announced .

The new project will include seven rounds, with equal prize money for women and men, and the promise of live broadcasts.

The series is built around growing Traka brand, and will leave several familiar stops from the Gravel Earth Series outside the new-look format.

Stages races Migration Gravel Race and Oregon Trail Gravel Grinder, as well as The Hills and Ranxo Gravel are among the events absent.

The Traka debuted in 2019 in Spain’s Girona region, and has since grown into one of the marquee events on the world gravel racing calendar.

On the back of that success, promoters launched the Gravel Earth Series in 2022. It closed out its final season in 2026 with 11 events across six countries, with Specialized Off-Road teammates Mads Würtz Schmidt and Geerike Schreurs winning the elite titles.

The new slimmed-down format puts the Traka brand front and center.

The move comes after Klassmark partnered this summer with Grupo Godó , a Barcelona promoter behind the Titan Desert and Barcelona Marathon.

The biggest change for fans in 2027 could be the ability to watch live coverage for every round, though details are not finalized.

Prize money will include a series-wide purse of €76,000 (about $85,000), divided equally between women and men in the pro category.

Racing opens at Santa Vall in February. Girona’s Traka anchors the calendar on May 1, with Iowa’s CORE4 and Belgium’s The River among the later stops.

Another event outside Europe in April and a series-ending finale called The Last Dance have venues still to be confirmed.

There are few interesting twists to the new series worth mentioning.

Riders must register as either “pro” or “open” and remain in that category all season. Only pro riders will race for overall standings and prize money, but open riders will be classified in age groups in certain events.

Cross-gender drafting is banned. Pro riders cannot use headphones, phones, or radios, and outside assistance is limited to official zones. Riders may share food, water, and basic tools, but cannot swap out bicycles or other components.

Participation also counts toward future access to the headliner event, now called The Traka Girona. Riders earn one point for each “By The Traka” event completed to count toward entry for the 2028 and 2029 editions.

items.title: How Cyclists Can Start to Run Without Getting Catastrophically Injured
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Pro cyclists keep crushing crazy running performances in the winter – but riders should apply caution before they take off-training inspiration.
items.lbText:
Nothing screams “off-season” more than when pro cyclists start popping crazy running performances into your Strava feed.

Whether it’s Mathieu van der Poel blasting 10Ks while nose-breathing or Andreas Leknessund and Alexys Brunel obliterating half- and full-marathon races, the ride-to-run pivot is as seasonal as pumpkin-flavored everything .

But if you’re feeling inspired to do the same now the fondo season is over and the weather is turning grim, don’t lace up your runners just yet.

An overzealous new running regimen could leave you with DOMS so bad you’ve got to walk down stairs backward and might not be any benefit when you’re back on the bike.

There’s a reason why Tom Dumoulin waited to retire before he clipped off a sub-2:30 at the New York Marathon .

And even for the most experienced runners, the crossover benefit to cycling is still unproven. A marathon P.B. in winter won’t guarantee an FTP personal best in spring.

But what about the benefits for bone health? We hear your cries. Well, some pro trainers have thoughts on that, too.

Here’s what cyclists should know before they take up running this off-season.

We cover what the pros do, the risks and benefits for you, and how to start running without smashing your capacity to cycle.

“Pro cyclist does stupid-fast run” is like a meme that’s auto-posted every autumn.

Riders driven stir-crazy by weeks without structure, competition, and a mandate to stay away from the bike often lace up their trainers at this time of year for an annoyingly fast “jog.”

Adam Yates, Tom Pidcock, and Tiffany Cromwell are among the active pros who’ve laced rapid running performances in off-seasons past.

This year, Brunel of TotalEnergies and Leknessund of Uno-X Mobility stepped up to stoke the annual “cyclist runs fast” meme.

Brunel finished 20th at the Lille Marathon in a smokin’ fast time of 2:26 . Leknessund casually ran a 1:15 at the Amsterdam Half Marathon, despite having run little more than 100km in the past year.

Those are times even the most devoted enthusiast runner would lose all their toenails and get plantar fasciitis for.

Brunel and Leknessund’s cycling coaches might not have been so impressed.

Tudor Pro Cycling performance guru James Spragg told Velo that even the strongest pros tread a tightrope if they pivot to running too fast.

“Those guys can run very good times compared to regular runners because they’ve got that huge cardiovascular base. But they don’t have the mechanical adaptations, and that makes them very average against a world-class runner. And that’s also where the injury risk can come up,” Spragg said.

“Cyclists who suddenly cross over don’t have the shock resistance that’s built in the cartilage over time, or the tendon stiffness which gives you running efficiency. They are mechanical adaptations that you need to get from running,” Spragg said.

“Trying to go too far or too fast without those can be dangerous.”

Brunel and Leknessund appear to have built some running base before they blasted their recent races. Their injury risks might not have been extreme.

Riders who feel inspired to start running fall into a trap of pushing harder than their bodies, pampered by years of non-weight-bearing sport, can handle.

“The one thing we as coaches have in our ‘advantage’ with cyclists coming into running is normally they do one run, and then the DOMS protects them from themselves,” Spragg laughed.

“They run once and then don’t run again until the next off-season.”

Pros “have” to step away from the bike in autumn to reset themselves for the next season of self-flagellation.

Amateur riders don’t have 10 months of heinous workouts and 50kph racing to steel themselves for, but there’s a similar temptation to take a winter break.

Short, dank days, and the end of a season of fondos, races, and adventures can make bike rides feel pretty unappealing.

But if you’re considering taking up running as an off-season replacement, apply caution.

For beginners, the acute DOMS can be so devastating that a set of stairs can feel insurmountable. And more chronic conditions can crop up surprisingly fast. Tendinopathies will flare after even a fortnight of running beyond your experience.

The brutal demands of running are why any good training program will start with weeks of run-walk workouts.

These extra-easy “interval” sessions prepare the body for ground reaction forces more than three times a runner’s bodyweight. But be warned – they will do nothing for the fitness of even a moderately trained cyclist.

For noobs, the time investment is high, and the aerobic payoff is low.

Even veteran runners may feel little benefit when they return to the bike after spending winter pounding trails and tarmac – a recent study found no improvement in sport-specific performance if running and cycling were used to replace one another.

Because the mechanics simply don’t translate.

Even the most souplessed pedal stroke is a predominantly concentric (shortening/pushing) muscle contraction. Meanwhile, running incorporates an eccentric load into a push-pull motion that’s totally alien to even the strongest riders.

Running builds fitness, but it can only be expressed on the bike if you maintain the riding legs.

Riders who want to take up running to avoid the misery of the winter need to consider their longer-term goals.

If you’re in a rush to maintain bike fitness ahead of early-season challenges, look beyond the latest pair of Hokas.

The early run-walk protocols will wipe time off your schedule and do almost nothing for your aerobic capacity.

However, those who gamble by skipping those slightly embarrassing intervals are running toward injury.

Jayco-AlUla team trainer Peter Leo said the inefficiency of “learning” to run should give riders pause.…

items.title: Brandon McNulty Has the Rainbow Jersey. Is Grand Tour Leadership Next?
items.author: ahood
items.content: UAE boss Matxin still believes in McNulty’s grand tour potential. Could his rainbow season bring a chance to test it?
items.lbText:
McNulty took in an AS Roma soccer game last month after winning worlds. (Photo: Mairo Cinquetti/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Brandon McNulty won’t spend his entire season in the rainbow jersey fetching bottles for Tadej Pogačar .

That’s according to UAE Emirates-XRG boss Joxean Fernández Matxin, who said the American world champion will see opportunities to win in 2027. And he even hinted at the possibility of grand tour leadership.

“Yes, have no doubt that he will have freedom and his own opportunities,” Matxin told Eurosport .

The bigger question is where those chances might fall on the stacked super team roster built around Pogačar and rising star Isaac del Toro.

Matxin said UAE is committed to giving the 28-year-old Arizonan plenty of shots to honor the stripes next season. In fact, UAE already backed McNulty across the Italian fall classics , where he delivered his first win in the rainbow jersey at the Veneto Classic .

“People are now talking about Brandon McNulty as world champion, but in recent years he has been leader or co-leader in many of the races on his calendar,” Matxin said.

McNulty admits he will be taking pulls for Pogačar in the big races like the Tour de France, and he has no illusions that his new stripes will change the pecking order that much.

But even Pogi joked that he might be returning the favor for McNulty in a few select races.

For McNulty, the most intriguing part of his rainbow jersey season could be dipping his toes into grand tour leadership.

With strong time trialing and climbing skillset, he’s still seen as untapped potential across three weeks. Matxin said 2027 could give him a clearer pathway.

“We’ve also tried to see how far he can go in a grand tour,” Matxin told Eurosport . “In the end, for one reason or another, the stars haven’t all aligned for him, because I don’t believe he isn’t a grand tour rider.”

He pointed to the 2025 Giro d’Italia as an example of how quickly the hierarchy can shift. McNulty finished a career-best ninth overall at the 2025 Giro while helping Del Toro finish second overall.

“In fact, at last year’s Giro d’Italia we had two leaders, Adam Yates and Juan Ayuso, and two alternatives, Brandon McNulty and Isaac del Toro,” he said. “In the end, Del Toro emerged strongly and consistently, but McNulty could also have had the opportunity.”

Leading a grand tour wouldn’t be that far of a stretch. He’s already proven he can win shorter, week-long stage races, like the CRO Race, the Volta a Valenciana, the Tour of Luxembourg, and the Tour de Pologne.

With Pogacar all but certain to return to the Tour de France and likely the Vuelta a España as well, a shot at the Giro alongside Del Toro could be in the cards.

All that will be fleshed out in the coming weeks in the winter team camps.

McNulty’s worlds win in Montréal stunned many, and Matxin and the other UAE brass were half-expecting Del Toro to come up aces with Pogačar sitting out with injury.

Instead, it was Team USA’s superb tactics coupled with McNulty’s perfectly timed attack that won the day to deliver America’s first road world title since 1993 .

“It was a more open world championships. Because a rider like Tadej, simply by being there, imposes a certain way of racing,” Matxin said. “Brandon seized his chance.”

Matxin pointed to a key moment in the final lap when Tom Pidcock’s pursuit drew the lead chasers within a few seconds of McNulty. Instead of shutting down the move, the bunch sat up, and McNulty had the legs to power home the historic win.

“Brandon won, but if Pidcock had closed those six seconds and they caught him, maybe we’d be talking about [Matteo] Jorgenson having won,” Matxin said.

“McNulty has that ability to hold on. He’s a time trialist, a rider with unquestionable quality and a mentality for winning. When we target certain objectives, he generally very rarely falls short.”

McNulty now has the jersey and the promise of freedom. He said he’s dreaming of winning a Tour de France stage in the world champion’s jersey.

The question will be if UAE lets him chase something even bigger.

items.title: Why the Factor ONE Proves Specialized Needs a New Venge
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: Aerodynamic data is objective, but selling speed is entirely psychological. Specialized made a massive marketing mistake, and no one seems to be noticing.
items.lbText:
Welcome to Dropped , a new weekly road and gravel cycling newsletter from Velo that brings you the latest ideas we’re debating endlessly on group rides, and a look behind the scenes of our coverage.

I recently posted an article comparing the Specialized Tarmac SL9 and the Factor ONE . They are two of the most important road bikes of the last year (give or take) and the perfect foil for one another. Both are built to go fast, but they represent completely different philosophies of modern speed. Because I’ve had the opportunity to spend a lot of time on both, I wanted to answer the questions everyone is asking. This is all very straightforward stuff.

After I posted that story, I started reading the comments. I generally do my best to read everything across all the platforms where we post. But what I saw in the comments on this comparison was something I didn’t expect.

A lot of people think the Factor ONE is ugly. That’s expected. It looks nothing like most bikes and it is pushing about as far from the traditional silhouette as you can get for a road bike. When a design is that radical, it’s naturally going to turn some people off.

The simple explanation is that Factor wrapped the tube shapes around aerodynamic data and didn’t care much if the result looked weird. I could tell you that and move on, but I don’t think that’s the whole story. To see the reality, you have to look a little deeper at the feedback.

People calling it ugly was a given. What wasn’t expected is that most of those same critics openly acknowledged that the Factor ONE is the faster bike. You’d see things like, “The Factor might be faster, but it’s ugly,” or, “The Tarmac isn’t an aero road bike, it’s an all-rounder.”

Think about what that means for a second.

The Specialized Tarmac SL9 is one of the fastest road bikes to ever exist. Tour magazine tested it at 205 watts of drag in the wind tunnel at 45 km/h. That is exceptionally fast, but it actually sits outside of the top 12 bikes Tour has ever tested. The Factor ONE is indeed faster with a baseline score of 202 watts, and by optimizing it with different wheels, aero tires, and a 1x configuration, Tour was able to push that number down to 196.8 watts.

Objectively, that is a win. But you also have to think about how aerodynamic drag works. Tour tests at 45 km/h (about 28 mph) because that’s the practical floor for testing. If you go any slower, you start getting into the margin of error for the wind tunnel and the results get muddy. But what about you and me? Over 100 to 300-mile distances, my average speed tends to sit at a weirdly specific 16.7 mph. On a normal day, I actually cruise closer to 20 mph. If I am pushing hard on a shorter ride, anything sustained past a few minutes might see me hold a best of 24 mph.

At those real-world speeds, the physics change dramatically. Looking at the absolute best-case scenario for the Factor (the fully optimized 1x setup, similar to how I run my size 54 with a SRAM XPLR drivetrain and Zipp 454/858 NSW wheels). At 24 mph, we are looking at roughly a 5-watt advantage over the Tarmac. That is still something to be impressed with, although remember it did take some work after it came from Factor. Drop to a 20 mph cruise, and that gap shrinks to just 3 watts. Drop it to my long-distance average of 16.7 mph, and the aerodynamic advantage essentially disappears completely.

So, there is virtually zero watt savings at 16.7 mph, but there is a very real penalty on the scale. When I weighed both bikes ready-to-ride minus pedals, the Tarmac was a full kilogram lighter. That’s 6.5kg for the Tarmac versus 7.57kg for the ONE. Is the ONE actually faster?

None of this is an indictment of the very real speed Factor has wrestled from the ONE. I believe in stacking aerodynamic efficiency and finding watts wherever I can. In fact, if I had to choose between the two bikes, I’d pick the ONE (and I said as much in the comparison article). I understand that across a long ride, we spend the vast majority of our time at lower gradients, meaning aerodynamic benefits lead to a faster overall ride. We also harvest larger gains when we push the pace, even if those advantages shrink when we slow down.

The point is simply that Specialized is technically correct in the philosophy they are using as a guiding principle. The Tarmac isn’t the absolute fastest in the wind tunnel, but Specialized rightly points out that trading a few watts to save a full kilogram is a highly valid equation. The brand is also looking at racing holistically: when you are drafting in a pack, you lose many of the aerodynamic advantages that come from an aggressive frame profile anyway.

Another way to look at this is strictly as a consumer and not a WorldTour racer. I ride alone a lot, which is why I love focusing on aero performance. But if you ride in a group, it’s incredibly common to just cruise and chat on the flats, only to turn the hills into a race. In that real-world scenario, you legitimately might want to optimize for climbing, because that’s the only time you are actually competing. Or, you might just prefer the snappy feel of a light bike.

Which is all to say: the idea that the Factor is definitively faster isn’t really true. It is faster in some scenarios and slower in others.

What’s important, though, is that people believe it’s faster. The shape of the bike is the marketing. When you look at the Factor ONE and think, “That’s ugly, but it must be fast,” that visual leap is all that matters. Perception is reality, and the perception is that Factor owns speed.

And this is where Specialized is losing. The brand is the only one in the industry that owns its own wind tunnel, yet somehow consumers look at the modern lineup and assume the innovation has stalled. Perception sells bikes, and that is a long-term problem.…

items.title: Redshift Releases Look and Shimano Compatible Mousetrap Pedal Adapters. Right Now They’re 25% Off.
items.author: Will Tracy
items.content: These adapters turn your clipless pedals into flat pedals in seconds.
items.lbText:
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside. Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Redshift Mousetrap pedal adapters (Photo: Redshift)

I’ll just say this up front: you don’t explicitly need Redshift’s Mousetrap pedal adapters. But then again do you really need most things out there? When I first saw these adapters that turn your clipless pedals into flat pedals, I wasn’t a hater, but I wasn’t convinced of their necessity, or who they are for. Who they are for, as it turns out, is me.

I keep SPD pedals on my around-town bike because it lets me go out and shred a little harder on any trip whether I’m grabbing groceries, visiting a friend, or just catching the sunset after work. But I don’t always want to put on riding shoes.

Can I get away with just riding with regular shoes on SPD pedals? Certainly, and I did it for years. Is life better now that I have these simple flat-pedal converters to toss on in seconds when I want them? Also certainly yes. The pedal platform for these is wide, grippy, and level—more than I can say for riding SPDs with regular shoes.

I’m not going to try to convince you that everyone needs these—you either have a use for them in your life or you don’t. You can pedal a bike with clipless pedals and regular shoes for quick trips around town no issue. But if you find yourself doing that regularly, the Mousetrap converters are a nice thing to have. It also means you can convert pedals in seconds, rather than maybe a couple minutes to swap in flat pedals. When you lay it out like that, it’s not a lot of time, but it is enough of a hassle that most of us, myself included, wouldn’t do it.

Now, Redshift is releasing the adapters for Look and Shimano SPD-SL road pedal styles. It’s essentially the same product, just modified to fit different pedal styles. Like with the SPD version, these adapters use the clip-in mechanism of your pedal to sit flush with the top of the pedal, provide an 80x105mm textured platform for grip, and clip on and off in seconds. When you’re not using them, a built-in magnet keeps them together so you don’t lose one between rides. There’s only a slight variation in weight between the versions due to their different clip-in mechanisms.

I just got a set of the SPD-SL version as well which I plan to keep in my car for when I drive to a ride with my road bike. Again, it’s not solving a huge problem in my life, but I’ll be plenty happy to have them for riding to lunch after the main ride.

Right now, Redshift is offering all three versions of the Mousetrap—SPD, SPD-SL, and Look—for 25% off as part of its early Black Friday Sale. Normally $59.99 USD, they are $44.99 right now.

Redshift says Crankbrothers Egg Beater pedals are next in the pipeline. Those pedals are definitely harder to ride with regular shoes, so I see even more of a use-case here for people who like the four-sided design.

items.title: What Could Cervélo, Beats, Rapha, and Bose Tell Us About Cannondale’s Future?
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: When iconic companies leave their roots, they usually leave something behind. What does this mean for one of cycling’s most beloved brands?
items.lbText:
Cannondale is packing up its Connecticut headquarters and leaving the state where it was founded 55 years ago. As parent company Pon.Bike consolidates North American operations into California, the brand is losing its historic home. What will this mean for a storied American brand?

Before I started writing for Velo , I spent over 20 years working for ad agencies as a creative director, making ads for some of the biggest brands in the world, including Samsung, Pepsi, IBM, and more. If you ever watched the TV show Mad Men, I was Peggy. Did I have a lot of martini lunches? That’s a story for another day.

​My job was to create ads that emotionally connected with consumers, protecting the most important asset these Fortune 500 companies had—their brand. So when I read the news about Pon.Bike closing Cannondale’s U.S. headquarters and consolidating operations within its portfolio, I paused.

Cannondale is closing its U.S. headquarters in Wilton, Connecticut. According to Bicycle Retailer, that means all 143 employees located there will be affected. Sales and operations are reportedly consolidating to Pon.Bike’s other American location in Santa Cruz, CA, where the holding company already has sales teams that handle the Cervélo and Santa Cruz Bicycles brands. Cannondale’s global HQ will relocate to Woudenberg, Netherlands. And R&D will remain in Freiburg, Germany, where it has operated for several years. According to reports, the first moves begin December 21, 2026, and will run in phases through the end of 2027.

​But a headquarters isn’t a brand. It’s a building. So nothing should really change, right? Maybe. For the Cannondale brand, I think it’s more than that.

The Cannondale story starts in 1971 in Wilton, Connecticut, where Joe Montgomery and Murdock MacGregor began making bike bags and trailers, pouring the proceeds into bike frames. They named those creations Cannondale, inspired by the nearby Metro-North train station.

​What came next was fifty years of bravado and innovation, building cycling curiosities that pushed the industry and grabbed people’s attention, for better or worse. From the Lefty fork (a single-sided suspension fork that soon became the stuff of legend) to the Hollowgram crankset (an ultra-light, super-stiff crank with an innovative two-piece bonded, hollow aluminum construction). Some ideas were more successful than others, but each carried that underdog spirit, the same scrappiness reminiscent of the organization’s early days.

​So what’s the secret sauce? Companies that create truly unique products do so by cultivating a culture of creativity. An environment where ideation and execution are celebrated, even if it is a little unorthodox. Originality is fueled by freedom. The space to dream up something different, weird, and unconventional. Sometimes that dream defines a category like the Synapse, blazing a trail for the endurance road bike category. Sometimes it’s a little less spectacular, like the familiar creak of the BB30 bottom bracket. Cannondale’s pioneering spirit had a home on the East Coast, and now, that space is being broken apart and shipped all across the world. Which begs the question…

To say exactly what the future holds for Cannondale is anyone’s guess. However, as a marketer, that’s where I turn to the next best thing…case studies. I looked at a variety of brands to see what happens when a company is ripped from its roots, when founders leave, and when they stick to their guns.

If you hark back to 2006, you’ll remember Beats by Dre, a Los Angeles headphone company started by the one and only Dr. Dre and longtime head of Interscope Records, Jimmy Iovine. While Beats sold headphones, they exported the energy of LA. The brand was steeped in West Coast hip-hop culture. The products looked amazing, sounded great, and consumers agreed, big time. Bloomberg Businessweek reported that at its peak in 2011, Beats held 64% of the U.S. premium headphone market. Then, in 2014, Apple acquired Beats for $3 billion. Dre and Iovine eventually left, and before long, the brand fizzled. LA energy gave way to Silicon Valley tech. Where’s the brand today? You can still buy Beats within the Apple ecosystem, but the revenue numbers are hard to pin down. In earnings calls, Apple doesn’t break out Beats revenue. Perhaps that’s all you need to know: a cultural giant reduced to a line item too small to report.

​Meanwhile, another headphone manufacturer is Bose. The company never sold. They never left their headquarters in Framingham, Massachusetts. And Dr. Amar Bose, founder and MIT professor, even gave the majority of the non-voting shares to the university where he taught for over 40 years. Why? He believed that a publicly held company could never innovate the same way that a private one could. So he gave the shares away. This is a story of commitment, principles, and, most importantly, what happens when founders stick to their vision, stay planted in their corporate roots, and weave their philosophy and vision into the brand’s fabric. While revenue numbers aren’t publicly reported, we can rely on the fact that Bose has outlasted every acquisition wave in the audio industry. Still independent, still in Framingham, and still the brand synonymous with great audio.

It would be impossible to do this article without talking about Rapha. What started in 2004 as Simon Mottram’s love letter to cycling culture, style, and functionality then exploded into a consumer obsession, with annual reports showing Rapha’s revenue growing 25–30% year over year, ending January 2017 at £63 million. According to The Guardian, Walmart’s Walton family stepped in and acquired the brand for a reported £200 million (approximately $254 million USD at the time). Mottram stepped down as CEO in 2021. And since the buyout, Rapha has not posted a single profitable year, reporting nine consecutive annual losses. Not to mention multiple CEOs and declining revenue.…

items.title: 78 Crashes and Pogačar Sidelined. UAE Has One Huge Ambition After Season of Carnage
items.author: ahood
items.content: A bruising season. A battered roster. Pogačar forced to stop. UAE’s response? Dreaming of winning all three grand tours in 2027.
items.lbText:
UAE's Matxin is dreaming big for 2027 despite a crash-filled season. (Photo: Getty Images)

UAE Emirates-XRG endured 78 crashes and fractures to more than half its roster, including world No. 1 Tadej Pogačar , in a season of unprecedented carnage for cycling’s super team in 2026.

UAE’s response? Team boss Joxean Fernández “Matxin” wants an even stronger Pogačar and a clean sweep of cycling’s three grand tours.

Pogačar’s season-ending Vuelta a España crash was the biggest blow in an injury-ravaged campaign that still produced 78 victories from 20 riders despite a season filled with spills, injuries, and broken bones.

“This year we’ve had very bad luck with crashes. We’ve had 78 crashes. Eighteen of our 30 riders have suffered fractures,” Matxin told Eurosport . “I think all those circumstances have made us strong and pushed us to surpass ourselves.”

By Matxin’s count, those 78 wins came with 78 crashes, meaning that UAE’s season produced as many victories as wipeouts, with fractures affecting more than half its roster.

Despite the endless wave of crashes, the team still ended 2026 ranked No. 1 in the world and won more races than any squad in the WorldTour.

That’s well off its record haul of 97 wins in 2025, however, showing just how devastating crashes were across cycling’s richest team.

Even after the bruising season, Matxin is raising the bar for 2027 with the ambition of winning the Giro d’Italia, Tour de France, and Vuelta in the same season.

“What am I longing for right now? I won’t lie to you: what Visma achieved, winning the Giro, Tour and Vuelta in the same year,” he said.

That assumes a healthy Pogačar is back in 2027 and the team can avoid a repeat of the costly spills.

Things were worse behind the scenes than many realized.

Matxin also revealed how UAE team doctor Adrian Rotunno pumped the brakes on Pogačar’s return to racing this fall.

The Slovenian initially hoped to return for the European championships after his devastating Vuelta crash.

Rotunno and the team’s medical staff were firm in advising that his racing season was over, and Matxin now credits them with making the right call.

“The medical team, led by Adrian Rotunno, was very firm in advising that his year was over,” Matxin told Eurosport .

“On the sporting side, you’re always thinking about whether he can make it back, whether he can win,” he said. “But the medical team’s clear-headed approach determined that the best thing was to end his season so we wouldn’t take any risks.”

Pogačar was champing at the bit to return to racing on the Euros on home roads in Slovenia just weeks after he crashed out of the Spanish grand tour, but later scans proved that ending his season and focusing on recovery was the prudent call.

“I think it was a wise decision and I have to thank them for it, because from my sporting perspective, you’re probably always looking at when he can return and be available,” Matxin said.

Pogačar is now training on open roads and looks to be on track for a full recovery.

But Pogačar’s own account underlines how bad things were. The Slovenian revealed to The Athletic last week that further scans uncovered two additional fractured vertebrae after his August 29 Vuelta crash.

“When I saw I had three broken vertebrae? I’m just happy to be alive, actually, or just to be standing,” he told The Athletic .

Matxin now sees the forced stop only fueling King Pog’s ambitions for 2027 .

“I have no doubt that Pogačar will be better than last year,” Matxin said.

There is some speculation that Pogačar could be a different rider after the high-speed Vuelta crash, but Matxin said he doesn’t expect him to lose any of his winning edge in the aftermath of the Slovenian’s first major injury.

“When you go through difficult moments and suffer, you savor the good moments more and make more of them,” he said. “I think you have to take something positive from everything in life, and in the bad moments you have to know that you’re going to come back stronger, with that little bit of anger that helps you improve.”

Matxin also brushed aside the idea of focusing solely on breakout French star Paul Seixas as Pogačar’s biggest Tour threat .

“You can’t rule out Remco. You can’t rule out Jonas. And obviously you can’t rule out Paul Seixas, because he has made such a brilliant breakthrough,” he said.

As for suggestions of an “anti-Pogačar” Tour route , Matxin understands why organizers want to keep the fight for yellow alive.

“What the organizers are looking for, and I understand them here, is to make sure the Tour isn’t decided by the fourth stage,” he said. “I understand that perspective.”

Matxin didn’t reveal any firm calendars yet for 2027, but if the grand tour sweep is on the radar, that would suggest that Isaac del Toro could head to the Giro d’Italia while Pogačar might repeat the Tour-Vuelta double.

There’s also talk that he might skip Paris-Roubaix, and emphasis on knocking off a record sixth yellow jersey and a first Vuelta to complete the grand tour sweep.

Those details will be sorted in the coming weeks at the team’s winter camps in Spain in December.

items.title: Zwift Clears Up the Stink of its Rogue Pooper with Hilarious New Update
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Zwift rushes out new graphics and segments to distract from footage of 'a guy taking a dump' in its premium real-world video package.
items.lbText:
Zwift has wiped away the mess left by an unfortunate addition to its new premium subscription tier.

On Tuesday, developers rushed through a “When You Gotta Go” sprint segment and built virtual barriers to distract from “a guy taking a dump” in its new real-world video playthrough.

Images of a rogue pooper had made it onto Zwift’s costly new premium package.

The online training giant rolled out its Zwift Plus tier on a wave of hype and promises of “the most powerful experience to date” last week.

Only Zwift’s costly new model didn’t get headlines for the platform’s first-ever real-life playthrough or personalized coaching system.

On Monday, Zwift rider Sam Sky noticed a figure crouched in the roadside bushes of the virtual Colorado River Sunrise route.

There was only one thing they could be doing – and Sky made sure to point it out on a Facebook post that’s since gone viral.

“Zoom in on the green circle. I saw a guy taking a dump by the side of the road during my session this morning on the new videos,” Sky wrote alongside a now-infamous screencap he shared on the Zwift Ride Owners Group.

A deluge of bad jokes ensued, and as Sky told Canadian Cycling Magazine , “I got a ton of comments on the photo I posted and over 1,000 likes in less than 24 hours.”

Zwift promised to clear up the mess ASAP, and duly issued its hilarious new update less than a day later.

Zwift super-nerd Eric Schlange revealed the new addition Tuesday on his independent Insider website:

“Yesterday, a Zwifter shared in Zwift Riders that they’d spotted someone taking a nature break 4.5km into the Colorado River Sunrise route,” Schlange wrote.

“Zwift responded within a few hours by erecting new road barriers to block the view… and by adding a new sprint segment called ‘When You Gotta Go!’ Amazing.”

It dropped the ball by letting a dude do a dump on its biggest upgrade in years, owned the mistake, and added its own touch of humor to clear up the stink.

items.title: Bianchi’s €100 Million Lesson: You Can’t Mass-Produce Heritage
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: Bianchi built a volume-focused factory when it should have protected its prestige. Here is why the world's oldest bike brand must pivot its strategy and return to what it does best.
items.lbText:
A Bianchi bicycle factory worker works on a bicycle in Treviglio, Italy. Bianchi is known for its racing bikes. | Location: Treviglio, Italy. (Photo by James L. Amos/Corbis via Getty Images) (Photo: Getty Images)

Bianchi is in trouble right now. First came the news that Bianchi is out of the WorldTour , and then we heard that the brand had entered into financial restructuring with €100 million in debt after losing €28 million between 2023 and 2025. How did the world’s oldest continuous bicycle manufacturer land itself in this spot, and what could possibly help?

In the heady days of the pandemic bike boom, Bianchi made a big strategic investment. With consumer demand surging and global supply chains in chaos, the brand decided to reshore its infrastructure in late 2021. It was not a small bet. Bicycle Retailer reported a €40 million ($45 million) investment to build a 30,000-square-meter (325,000-square-foot) facility. Roughly 17,000 square meters were devoted to bike production, creating a capacity of 1,000 bikes per day by 2023. The plan would increase employment from 180 to 250 personnel, prominently featured e-bikes in the strategy, and even included a museum.

These plans came from aggressive financial projections. According to Road.cc, Bianchi’s turnover was €50 million in 2018, but the brand expected growth to €120 million for 2021 and an unheard of €200 million by 2022. Much of this projected growth hinged on e-Omnia e-bike sales in the German and Italian markets, combined with a strong internal belief that it was the absolute right moment to return control of production to Italian shores.

As we all know now, Bianchi chose what might have been the absolute worst time in history to bring production back to Italy (or not but more on that shortly). The new Treviglio factory opened in June 2024, immediately becoming a black hole for cash just as the global cycling market cratered. As BikeItalia reported, “total operating costs exceeded €118 million, more than revenues. Personnel costs rose to €10.6 million to support a team of approximately 180 employees… Added to this are the depreciation of the plant and machinery.”

Instead of the projected €200 million by 2022, Bianchi reported €114.4 million in revenue for 2024. The brand saw growth, but nowhere near fast enough to become profitable with a massive factory and debts to service. Debts are sky-high, growth has stalled, and the company is in serious trouble.

If I were in charge of Bianchi—with no actual business acumen, mind you—I would have argued that reshoring production when it happened was actually a genius move. Well, almost genius. It was so close, but it completely missed the realities of the market.

Bianchi is never going to survive going head-to-head with the pricing and manufacturing scale that Chinese factories bring to the industry. XDS is massive, and its products are amazing. Bianchi cannot win that fight, but the brand has something those brands won’t have for at least another 20 years: a story.

Bringing production back to Italy is smart for supply chain reasons, but it is even smarter because it tells a better story. When your bikes are made in the same factories as everyone else’s, it’s to stand out. When you make your bikes in your own factory, in the exact same place you’ve been for longer than anyone else, you have a passion story. Unfortunately, you have to pair that passion with exclusivity, and that was the first mistake Bianchi made. Instead of scarcity, the brand reached for volume.

The second mistake was spreading too thin while delivering unremarkable halo products. Bianchi seems completely unable to make a decent gravel bike, operating with no real understanding of the modern market. On the road, the brand launched the latest Oltre and Specialissima with bold, polarizing designs. Unfortunately, the Oltre was too polarizing and, frankly, not that good. The previous Specialissima was pretty good— I wrote about loving it —but when it was time to launch the next generation, things went sideways. The latest Specialissima isn’t a climbing bike anymore, and it doesn’t really have a personality. It seems to exist as much to carry the Bianchi name as anything else.

Unfortunately, I was not in charge of Bianchi when someone was deluding themselves that the brand was poised to compete on volume with Asian manufacturing. Those decisions were made, and the fallout now has to be managed. In the short term, I imagine the hope is that a favorable agreement can be reached with creditors to get things back on track. Perhaps billionaire Ivan Glasenberg wants to add Bianchi to his Pinarello and Campagnolo portfolio and share that Treviglio factory space? Or perhaps not, but from my seat, I can see a path to at least selling bikes.

The first thing Bianchi has to understand is what the brand actually means to consumers. No one dreams of a Bianchi e-bike, and its gravel reputation needs serious rehabilitation. The core road lineup has to carry the weight, which means the Oltre needs to immediately be very good. It is already a weird-looking bike; let that be, but take a note from Factor and turn it into an asset. Let it look weird so it’s distinctive, but don’t lose what matters: it has to be fast, and it has to ride incredibly well.…

items.title: Roglič Is Running Out of Time: The Era’s O.G. Has No Contract and Few Options
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Primož Roglič suffers another setback in his search for a ride for 2027 as forced retirement becomes increasingly likely for a modern great.
items.lbText:
(Photo: Marco BERTORELLO / AFP via Getty Images)

Everyone’s obsessed with what’s next for Paul Seixas, but shouldn’t we be thinking more about Primož Roglič ?

The modern era’s grand tour OG is out of contract with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, and he’s running out of time to secure his future.

Having been linked to seemingly half the teams in the pro peloton , Roglič’s options are becoming increasingly thin.

According to contract super-sleuth Daniel Benson, a previously muted link up with Tom Pidcock at Pinarello-Q36.5 is now off the table. Benson reported the news Wednesday on Twitter / X .

If correct, that will be another team crossed off the list of options for a rider who clearly has more to give.

Roglič dogged out second place at the Vuelta a España in September before he bounded to an unforeseen European time trial title one month later.

Despite Roglič’s late-season resurgence and his ongoing will to race into 2027, he’s accepted his days might be numbered.

“You never know when is the last [race],” Roglič said last month before he finished 10th at Il Lombardia.

When pressed on whether he will continue to race next year, Roglič said, “I don’t know yet. We will see. We will see.”

Benson’s reporting on Wednesday makes it seem increasingly likely that “The Race of the Falling Leaves” was Roglič’s last dance, whether he likes it or not.

“What’s next for Roglič” has become a saga worthy of its own Box Set.

He was linked to Lotto-Intermarché way back in summer but reportedly turned down the Belgian team’s offer.

Since then, the five-time grand tour winner has variously been connected to Unibet Rose Rockets, Tudor Pro Cycling, and his former team, Visma-Lease a Bike.

Het Laatste Nieuws reported last week that initial talks between Roglič and Visma have been called off.

Unibet Rose Rockets founder Bas Tietema revealed he had contact with Roglič ahead of the Vuelta a España, but made no suggestion of intent.

And the chances of a move to Tudor are looking increasingly slim – though Fabian Cancellara’s ambitious young team does still have a space on its roster.

With Pinarello-Q36.5 seemingly out of the running, Roglič’s time – and options – are running out.

Roglič may be without a contract for next year, but the four-time Vuelta a España champion and Giro d’Italia winner still holds some star power.

The Slovenian will do the rounds as a special guest at the Taiwan Masters Ride on Monday, November 9.

He and a selection of B-tier pros will be joined by a mob of local fans in a ride outside of Taipei.

But who knows, that could be Roglič’s last ride as a pro.

It would be a strange way to bow out for a rider who’s been so definitive of the modern era.

Having turned 37 just last week, Rogla is one of the few survivors of the pre-pandemic age – a time of rim brakes and 175mm cranks – to have remained competitive in his craft.

The riders who finished behind “the Slovenian who was a ski jumper” when he claimed his first Vuelta a España victory in 2019 reads like a pro cycling retirement home. Tadej Pogačar, then in his grand tour debut , is the one anomaly alongside Alejandro Valverde, Nairo Quintana, Rafal Majka, and the disgraced “superman” López.

In the seven years since Vuelta win No.1, Roglič has become the peloton’s enduring enigma, a rider who either crashes or crushes, and who says everything and nothing all at once.

With 93 wins on his palmarès, he’s one of the most celebrated riders in the bunch. Pogačar is the only active pro to have won more.

Roglič is far from his peak. With only two wins in 2026, this was the least successful year of his pro career.

But he’s refused to be pushed out of the picture altogether.

His defiant home victory at Ljubljana’s European time trial championships proves that point.

“It’s beautiful, it’s of course for me, but it’s also for all the people,” Roglič said after he accepted the white-and-blue Euro jersey.

“My radio stopped working. It cut out in the first kilometer of the race, so I was completely lost,” he added. “I just went with my instincts.”

Roglič’s European TT victory was as unlikely as it gets.

He might need to pull something equally unlikely to be able to wear that champion’s jersey in 2027.

items.title: Want to Own Pogačar’s Winning Bike? It’s Up for Auction in LA28 Push
items.author: ahood
items.content: Pogačar’s winning Colnago and McNulty’s rainbow jersey: Bid for cycling history and help fuel America’s LA28 medal push.
items.lbText:
Pogačar's winning bike is up for auction to help USA Cycling. (Photo: MAARTEN STRAETEMANS / Belga / AFP)

Tadej Pogačar ’s monument-winning bike and Brandon McNulty’s signed rainbow jersey headline a USA Cycling Foundation auction opening Wednesday to help fund America’s push for medals at Los Angeles 2028 .

Fans worldwide can bid on the Colnago V5Rs that Pogačar rode to victory at the 2025 Liège-Bastogne-Liège, alongside a world champion’s jersey signed by his UAE teammate McNulty.

McNulty’s world title in Montréal has given American road cycling fresh momentum heading toward its first home Olympics since Atlanta 1996 .

Officials say the challenge now is to turn that rainbow breakthrough into Olympic hardware .

“Our athletes are proof of what private support can do,” said foundation executive director Molly Pickall. “LA28 is the first Summer Games on home soil since 1996, and we want to arrive with the strongest team we’ve ever fielded.”

The foundation’s fifth annual online auction runs November 4-9, with bidding closing at 6 p.m. Pacific time. Proceeds support programs that identify, develop, and prepare U.S. Olympic and Paralympic cyclists.
