items.title: Vingegaard’s Dilemma: Chase Another Giro or Risk Everything Against Pogačar?
items.author: ahood
items.content: Analysis: The Giro looks made for Vingegaard. But would defending pink leave him running on fumes against Pogačar at the Tour de France?
items.lbText:
Will Vingegaard return to the Giro or bet everything on the Tour? (Photo: Getty Images)

The Giro d’Italia just gave Jonas Vingegaard plenty of reasons to return in 2027 with a route that keeps pointing uphill.

A mountain time trial, the Mortirolo and Gavia, and a penultimate showdown on Monte Zoncolan serve up the defending champion a near-perfect course to defend pink as Visma-Lease a Bike maps out his return from a season-ending crash.

The Tour de France ? Some are calling it the Anti-Pogačar Tour , but in many ways, it looks even less inviting for Vingo.

With just three summit finishes and 71km of individual time trialing, the 2027 Tour offers fewer chances for the Dane to turn the screws with his Pogi-killer climbing power that delivered his two yellow jerseys.

So heading into the winter team camps, Visma and Vingegaard face a season-deciding quandary.

Would another run at pink give him a better chance of winning a grand tour in 2027 before another July clash with Tadej Pogačar ?

Or would another Giro take too much out of him and leave him empty in his pursuit of yellow?

The urgent question facing the Visma brain-trust now is how to win another grand tour while also giving Vingegaard his best shot at beating Pogačar.

Vingegaard is being squeezed from all directions as the 2026 season is a wrap.

He’ll be 30 in December, Pogačar remains his bête noire , and a new generation of GC riders is nipping at his heels.

King Pog keeps raising the bar in front of him, and after signing a blockbuster contract extension , he isn’t going anywhere. Behind him, Remco Evenepoel , Isaac del Toro, and Paul Seixas are pumping new hype and ambition into the grand tour conversation.

The Dane who twice beat Pogačar at the Tour now finds himself defending his place as the Slovenian’s most dangerous rival.

Vingegaard boasts four grand tour victories, yet some are already writing him off as the best candidate to crack the Pogačar code.

That’s a strange place to be for someone who ran away with the pink jersey just a few months ago.

And it puts huge pressure on Visma and Vingegaard for the choices they have to make for 2027.

Another pink jersey would underline how good he still is. A third yellow would silence those already writing him off.

So far, neither Vingegaard nor his team is giving much away.

Visma’s official reaction Tuesday to the Giro route offered zero clues. Head of racing Marc Reef praised the course without revealing the team’s plans for 2027.

“To win this Giro d’Italia, you need to have a wide range of qualities. That makes it a really exciting challenge,” Reef said. “We will study the route carefully before putting together the best possible plan.”

This year, Visma and Vingegaard took plenty of heat for attempting the Giro-Tour double.

The first part worked like a charm, with Vingegaard riding away with pink to complete the grand tour sweep.

The Tour went off the rails when he gave up time to Pogačar in the first week and then crashed out on stage 15 with a broken clavicle. He hasn’t raced since.

Team boss Richard Plugge told TV2 after the Tour reveal last month that the yellow jersey remains the central goal for the Killer Bees.

Whether a Giro defense fits into that calculation remains the big question.

Never one to go over the top on social media or give too many interviews, Vingo is leaving everyone guessing about his grand tour plans. No decisions have been announced.

Vingo remains the only rider to beat Pogačar at the Tour, winning in 2022 and 2023. Since then, the Slovenian has been unstoppable with three straight yellow jerseys, but Vingegaard has never given up.

Yet some are already suggesting that he will have a hard time even hitting the Tour podium in 2027 on a course that, on paper, doesn’t favor his strengths.

Ex-pro Michael Rasmussen believes the time trial-heavy, summit-light Tour route reflects the evolving hierarchy inside the elite men’s peloton.

“I don’t think ASO still sees Vingegaard as Pogačar’s main challenger,” Rasmussen said on Viaplay . “I see more potential in the riders coming up behind him.”

Yet fewer summit finishes don’t mean Vingegaard won’t a fighting chance for yellow.

He’s not that bad at time trialing, and the Tour still includes a late showdown on Col du Portet featuring the Tourmalet and 5,400m of climbing. That’s Vingegaard’s happy place.

And who could have guessed Pogačar would have crashed out of the Vuelta a España?

Visma remains one of the most successful teams of the decade, with grand tour victories hard-wired into its DNA. It won’t give up on yellow easily.

The ultimate question for Vingegaard and Visma is what matters more: winning another Giro or going all in for a third yellow jersey?

That could make for a few sleepless nights inside the Visma bus.

There’s another wrinkle: This year’s Giro-Tour bet ended without a clear resolution for the brain-trust inside the Visma bus.

Visma won the opening team time trial in Barcelona, but Vingegaard steadily lost time and then crashed out two weeks later at the foot of the Alps. And even though he was already four minutes-plus behind Pogačar, the team’s data wizards never got the final week of racing to complete their assessment.

Missing from much of this discussion is Vingegaard himself.

The last official team update came on August 17, when Visma confirmed Vingegaard wouldn’t race again this year. Since then, it’s been crickets and his 2027 program remains under wraps.

It’s hard to imagine Vingo not racing the Tour.

He’s Visma’s marquee grand tour leader, and winning the yellow jersey remains the assignment. And King Pog already confirmed where he will be in July.

Would going back to the Giro be read as waving the white flag for July? Some will inevitably see it that way.

But betting everything on the Tour and coming back empty-handed carries its own risk.

Repeating the double in 2027 would come with the same risk and potential reward.…

items.title: Giant Revolt Advanced SL Review: A Gravel Race Bike Perfect for the Modern Era
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: Giant's new flagship gravel race bike is lighter, stiffer, and offers top-level handling in a bike built for 53mm tires.
items.lbText:
Lightweight frame construction and build options

Progressive geometry, including longer chainstays that promote strong handling characteristics

Increased horizontal stiffness to promote responsiveness and more precise control

A few wonky spec choices, including only a setback seat post

The Giant Revolt Advanced SL is the latest update to the popular Revolt line. The new bike focuses on being a lighter bike with improved geometry, increased stiffness, and refined components. All of these qualities are geared to promote better handling and more speed over rough terrain with large tires.

The bike debuted as a prototype at Unbound 200, snagging a top-five finish in the men’s race. In a race where the rest of the top five was filled with the Specialized Crux 5—the other new release at Unbound—that initial showed the racing chops of the new offering from Giant.

While the Revolt Advanced SL has had quick success at the races, we were curious to see how the pure-bred racer would fare for more varied terrain. On paper, the Revolt was a bike that didn’t have the same compliance and suspension features as other bikes in our gravel bike Field Test . The gravel riding in Squamish would test the limits of what the bike could do away from the race course.

What we found was that the bike was not only fast, but through smart geometry decisions and lightweight, responsive terrain, the Giant Revolt outkicked expectations across even the rougher terrain we took on.

The Revolt has never been the most audacious gravel bike on the market, yet Giant has consistently been a standard bearer each time it gets updated. Even last year, the previous Revolt, already a few years old, stood out as one of the best options in our 2025 gravel bike field test.

This time around, the new and improved Revolt only impressed us more. The high points are things we have seen across the board in new gravel bikes this year: bigger tires, a lighter frame, more aerodynamic shaping. Yet, in a few key ways, it is the details and design beyond the big headlines that are the most exciting aspects of the new Revolt.

That being said, straightaway, the lightweight frame and speed of the bike were the most obvious features. The bike we tested came in as the lightest bike of our test by a big margin. At just 17.3 pounds (7.84 kg), the bike accelerated fast and was able to hold speed well. Giant claims that the bike has a 13.81-watt aerodynamic improvement over the previous Revolt. With the low weight and the aero-shaping, the Revolt felt like a race bike, especially on smooth and uphill terrain.

Adding to that racey feeling was the bike’s stiffness. In a bit of a zag compared to where most gravel bikes are headed, Giant made it a priority to boost the frame’s stiffness. The idea here is that compliance can be found in other components—more on that later—but a rock-solid power platform needs the grounding of a stiff frame and cockpit. The Revolt demonstrates that stiffness during moments of high power, both seated and standing. With tires that take advantage of the bike’s improved clearance, those qualities make the bike such a good climbing option.

The ability of the Revolt as a climbing bike seems obvious, even on paper. What was more surprising was how well the Revolt was able to handle descending and rougher terrain, even with a stiff, fully rigid setup.

After a few miles to get used to the bike, I felt a ton of stability on a wide variety of terrain. At speed, I felt a ton of responsiveness, but not twitchy. It was easy to place the bike, yet unlike other shorter, steeper bikes, the bike was super balanced and tracked well around corners. The length of the rear end, especially, prevents the bike from understeering.

Understeering, which happens when the rear wheel tracks tighter than the front wheel, is a common attribute of many new bikes with slack front ends and short chainstays. I have found it increasingly frustrating since it really holds certain bikes back from getting the most out of bigger tires. With 430+ chainstays, the Revolt handles bigger tires in a much more predictable way, which in turn manages traction better through both the front and rear tires.

All of this added together makes for a lightweight gravel race bike, with solid do-it-all capability, that is simply a joy to ride across the full spectrum of what gravel riding is known for.

The main aspect that I found frustrating about the Revolt is the proprietary seat post. Instead of a standard round post, the bike comes standard with a sweeping set-back D-shaped seat post. While the post does allow for a bit of compliance in the rear of the bike, it does create a bit of positional inflexibility.

That said, the bike does have a fairly steep seat tube angle to counteract that setback. Additionally, the Revolt does lower the stack and extend the reach of the previous versions of the frame. Yet, unlike other new releases, the Revolt has kept the reach of the bike at just 401mm for the medium-large frame we tested.

While Giant claims the seat post adds some compliance to the rear of the bike, overall, I was left wanting more compliance. The stiffness of the bike and the bars feels great at times, but over bumpier terrain the bike is less forgiving than I would like it to be. Bigger tires can certainly make up a lot of the difference, but pairing all of those stiff features with the very stiff Cadex wheels that come stock, and the stiffness adds up.

That said, it does give the bike a bit more upside as a do-it-all jack of all trades.

Lastly, while Giant argues that the bike’s components are updated to modern standards, I found that certain specs like crank length and bar width weren’t up to the standards of 2026. The 172.5mm cranks on our test bike were the longest in the Field Test, and I don’t think they reflect what most riders prefer to use.…

items.title: A Shimano Shoe Disaster, Bra Doping, and the 5 Biggest Controversies and Catastrophes of 2026
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: From Van der Poel's pedal meltdown at Roubaix to the beef-to-end-all-beefs at the Tour, these weird and wild moments blew up the cycling season.
items.lbText:
Wout van Aert’s emotional victory at Paris-Roubaix. Demi Vollering’s rout of road worlds. Tadej Pogačar’s crash ‘n’ comeback conquest of Milan-San Remo.

The 2026 cycling season was loaded with races for the ages.

It was sprinkled with plenty of controversies, catastrophes, and meme-worthy WTFs, too.

Remember Mathieu van der Poel’s pedal fiasco at Paris-Roubaix?

Or the beef-to-end-all-beefs between Demi Vollering and Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney at the Tour de France Femmes?

And there’s surely no forgetting Jonas Vingegaard’s dungaree-inspired solution to keeping toasty at Paris-Nice.

We’ve rewound through the bike-racing bloopers of 2026 to select the wildest, wackiest moments of the season. Strap in for a recap of mechanical meltdowns, dubious maneuvers, and some debate about “bra doping.”

One of the most hotly debated, sensationally divisive moments of this cycling season occurred away from the damning proof of TV cameras.

The Tour de France Femmes exploded into the biggest beef in recent memory when something happened between Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney and Demi Vollering’s superdomestique Célia Gery on stage 8 of the race.

Riding at the front of the pack, Gery, Vollering, and Niewiadoma blasted into a tight left-hand corner at the entrance to a decisive kicker climb.

Broadcast footage cuts from an overhead drone shot as the bunch dives under tree cover, and returns to a front-on moto camera shot a split second later.

The race tilted on its head in that one unseen moment.

According to Niewiadoma, Gery took her out of Vollering’s wheels as the Dutchwoman attacked. Niewiadoma was unable to respond and was blown out of the yellow jersey by the end of the stage.

“Gery on purpose just blocked me to the barriers where I had to stop pedaling,” Niewiadoma claimed.

“If they want to compete, they should compete fair play and not look for me to close me in the barriers,” Niewiadoma said. “I feel like it’s so childish.”

UCI commissaires had nothing to say. The cycling world was left attempting to piece together fragmented fan footage to figure it out.

Social media duly blew up with speculation and armchair sleuthing.

Gery was blasted by online death threats.

The final stage of the Femmes played out in the shadow of a volatile, bubbling beef between eternal rivals Niewiadoma and Vollering.

The two superstar riders attempted to turn down the volume on the controversy ahead of Vollering’s crowning stage 9 victory, but by then it was too late.

“Kasia Corner” had launched the Femmes beyond cycling media and onto the world stage.

Alpecin-Premier Tech showed the peloton how not to win Paris-Roubaix with smart tech choices this year.

Mathieu van der Poel and Jasper Philipsen threw away their podium chances in a meme-worthy cleat kerfuffle on the kingmaker cobbles of the Trouée d’Arenberg.

When three-time Roubaix champion MVDP punctured on the notorious stones, Philipsen selflessly handed his wingman his bike.

Philipsen was riding a prototype of Shimano’s new cleat-pedal system. Van der Poel and the rest of the team were rocking the standard-issue, outgoing set-up.

The two aren’t compatible , as MVDP was about to find out.

Clearly unaware of the mismatch, Van der Poel hopped onto Philipsen’s bike and optimistically pushed off onto the cobbles. After a few foiled attempts to clip in, the cobblestone crusher tossed aside the useless bike and walked forlornly back down the verge in hope of some help.

Meanwhile, Alpecin-Premier Tech’s Tibor del Grosso had been busy swapping an inflated wheel from his bike to Van der Poel’s original, discarded ride.

More than two minutes after his puncture, Van der Poel was back on a bike with two inflated tires, a pedal system that suited his cleats, and was chasing hard.

Any hope of a comeback didn’t last long. A few hundred meters later, Van der Poel flatted again.

Team boss Christoph Roodhooft stepped up after the race to cop the blame.

“Of course, that came together at an incredibly bad time. I never thought it would happen,” Roodhooft told Sporza . “We made the decision to use the pedals in race conditions.

“I never thought it would come together like this,” he said. “It is what it is. It won’t happen again, but it’s over now.”

Philipsen dutifully praised his team sponsor’s new shoes on Instagram when they officially launched this September.

“Finally, I can show you what I’ve been racing on all season. The new S-Phyre RC910 shoes and Dura-Ace PD-R9300 pedals,” Philipsen wrote alongside a Shimano promo reel.

“I’m proud to have played a part in their development.”

We wonder what Van der Poel thinks of them.

The only way to beat Demi Vollering in 2026 was to pray she took a wrong turn.

Vollering’s Hall of Fame season suffered its only blip this March when she and a whole horde of favorites took a wrong turn in the high-stakes denouement of Strade Bianche.

An attack group was around one minute up the road.

Only 33km remained to the iconic finale on the Piazza del Campo.

Vollering, Lotte Kopecky, Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, and Anna van der Breggen were in a small chase group with no time to lose.

Unfortunately, they all lost a lot of time when they mistakenly followed a race moto off course down a side track strewn with rocky boulders.

Vollering and Co. rattled down the stony path for a few hundred meters before realizing this was a level of sterrato far too extreme for Tuscany’s white-roads classic.

They pulled to a halt, awkwardly unclipped, waddled their bikes around a full 180, and returned to the race course. But by then, there was no coming back. They were three minutes behind the leaders and without hope.

Who was to blame for the off-course chaos? The moto or the riders?

The driver no doubt made a mistake, but riders are required to know the course.

Kopecky later admitted herd mentality prevailed in the heat of the chase.…

items.title: Why Our Performance-Obsessed Editor is Willing to Give Up 3 Watts for Giant’s New Helmet
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: It doesn't top the charts in isolated aero testing, but a small design tweak solves one of the most frustrating problems for fast riders.
items.lbText:
Breathability on par with vented helmets Visibility in an aero position Brow stays put when tightened Fidlock buckle

Lacking Virginia Tech Score Technically slower than other helmets

I am deeply interested in helmet aerodynamics for one simple reason: it is the cheapest wheel upgrade you can buy. While a lightweight, deep-section aero wheelset might cost upwards of $4,000, a high-end aero helmet normally costs in the $350 range but provides the same benefit. Going from shallow climbing wheels to deep aero wheels might save you about 10 watts, and that’s roughly the same as swapping your standard ventilated helmet for a fast aero road helmet. Go for both if you can, but if you have to pick one, it’s pretty obvious the helmet makes more sense.

More likely, though, in 2026, your bike already came with deep aero wheels and you still need a helmet. I always recommend picking an aero helmet for the free watts, but there are obviously other considerations. It has to keep you cool in the heat, it has to be safe, it has to be comfortable, and it has to look good.

After years of neglect, the Giant Pursuit got an unexpected update as we close in on the tail end of 2026. The tricky thing for every other helmet company right now is just how good the Specialized Evade 4—my current pick for best overall in the best bike helmets buyer’s guide —actually is. Because of that, I’ve almost started to expect less from other brands. Then the Giant Pursuit showed up, and I took it to Death Valley to ride in 30 mph winds and 109-degree temps. It was so good it was worth telling you about. Here’s why I am so impressed with the 2026 Giant Pursuit aero helmet.

Let’s clear up a lingering misconception: a modern aero helmet gives up nothing when it comes to ventilation. In 2026, brands use advanced internal channeling to capture air and pull it across your scalp as you move forward. When you slow down on a steep climb, it gets hot—but that is true whether your helmet is highly vented or completely solid. The Giant Pursuit is no different. I really did wear it in 109-degree heat through Death Valley. It was undoubtedly hot, but the more enclosed aero shell actually proved to be an advantage by keeping my scalp from getting sunburned.

Beyond the thermal management, my favorite feature of the Giant Pursuit is the field of vision in a deep aero tuck. With the Specialized Evade 4, as well as other options, I often struggle to get as low as I want while still seeing past the front brow of the helmet. Giant carved out just enough space at the front lip so you don’t have to crane your neck uncomfortably to see up the road.

Part of that is that the Pursuit also excels at stability. Over long miles, many helmets—aero or not—have a tendency to slowly slip down and rest against the top frame of my sunglasses. Giant designed a retention system that tightens down securely without creating pressure points on the forehead. It stays exactly where you put it, and the internal padding manages moisture well enough that when it finally saturates, the sweat drips clear of your lenses rather than blurring your vision.

This one is a little tricky, but what I ultimately don’t like is knowing this is not the absolute fastest helmet for me. I took a GiBLI G10 aero sensor out and tested this helmet directly against the Specialized Evade 4. Same day, same bike, same everything but the helmet. The difference was 3 watts at 25 mph, or 2 watts at 20 mph. I’m not going to sit here and say that’s a massive dealbreaker, but if I can pick between two good helmets and one is faster, why wouldn’t I? Ideally, the Pursuit would match the Evade 4’s speed while keeping that superior field of vision in an aero tuck. Perhaps that visibility is only possible because of the aerodynamic tradeoff, but I can wish.

I also wish we had a Virginia Tech test score. I suspect the helmet would do well simply because Mips-equipped helmets tend to score highly in the Virginia Tech testing protocol, but when you don’t have an answer, it remains an open question. For plenty of riders, that lack of third-party safety validation will be a far more serious issue than any potential wattage win or loss.

The main reason I wanted to write about the Pursuit helmet is essentially a livability detail, so I’ll say it again: the field of view in an aero tuck is excellent.

Beyond that, Giant is using a Fidlock buckle. I’ve included that in the pros, but that’s being very generous. It’s nice enough, but I’ve never once thought to myself that what I really needed was a magnetic buckle. It’s a solution to a problem that doesn’t exist.

On the other hand, the rear retention dial has gotten stuck once or twice and proven to be a little fiddly. For comparison, Specialized uses an FS2 BOA Fit System for the rear dial, and it’s excellent. Both Fidlock and BOA are third-party brands that require extra cash for inclusion. If I can only have one, I’d much rather see that budget spent on the BOA dial than the magnetic buckle. That said, none of this is a dealbreaker.

I recently ran a Velo Helmet Priority Poll asking what matters most when buying a helmet. Only 11 percent of respondents said their first priority is maximum aerodynamic performance and free watts. On the other hand, 45 percent said fit, comfort, and aesthetics are the ultimate deciding factors. You might think that means I suddenly have to back off aero as an important metric, but that’s not how I see it. The results actually make perfect sense to me, and it’s exactly how I would coach all aero-focused riders to think. Aero gains should never come at the cost of comfort. When an aero-focused product is designed right, that speed is an added benefit.…

items.title: What Makes This a Race Bike for Humans? Pivot Gets Into Road Bikes.
items.author: Will Tracy
items.content: Pivot Founder and CEO Chris Cocalis joins Mike Levy in this special episode of the Velo Podcast presented by Pivot.
items.lbText:
In this special episode of the Velo Podcast presented by Pivot, Chris Cocalis, Founder of Pivot Cycles, joins Mike Levy to discuss a new project from the Arizona, based brand.

Most people know Pivot for forward thinking mountain bikes, but now the brand is getting into road bikes with the Pravia, a bike Pivot is calling “a race bike built for humans.”

This is actually a return to road bikes for Pivot. The brand partnered with BH years ago on road bike product development and design from 2007 to 2012. Fast forward to today and Pivot has decided the time is right to get into this category under its own name.

“I just thought we could have a cutting edge product that was better,” said Cocalis.

For this project, he tapped into the innovative spirit at Pivot, like when the brand pushed into 29-inch wheels early, or developed a fat bike. “Pivot is our brand, and wherever we decide to take it we can compete in those categories,” he said.

Although there was some consideration for making a super lightweight, specialist bike, Cocalis really wanted to get back to having one good road bike to ride everything. So the Pivot team set forth to create the Pravia, a high-end road bike with elements that riders will find more comfortable, without sacrificing much in the way of performance. They have lovingly dubbed it “a race bike built for humans.”

Cocalis was deeply involved in the bike development process for the Pravia.

He walks us through the carbon layup development process. It took two years to get all the different sizes correct, and the 56 size around took at least six rounds of development to get the weight and ride quality where they wanted them. But it’s actually the smallest sizes that are the hardest to develop. Cocalis also talks to us about how Pivot’s Hollow Core Carbon Molding process for creating carbon frames differs from other brands. He calls it the most precise way to make a carbon frame.

Levy and Cocalis also get into the nitty gritty details that set this bike apart

Cocalis talked us through his decision to include downtube storage, a move that isn’t always perceived as being for performance bikes. It was also a massive development process to get a downtube storage door that “doesn’t squeak, doesn’t creak, doesn’t leak,” and that’s before trying to hit stiffness and weight targets. It’s part of the reason they needed six rounds of layup development on the size 56 frame alone.

Cocalis then discusses the decision to go all-in on electronic shifting. As he puts it, the Pravia is a high-end bike built for a rider that’s not interested in mechanical shifting. And making it electronic only means not sacrificing ride quality, performance, or weight to build in cable guides and stops. “It is definitely a performance minded decision,” Cocalis said.

Then there’s the small details that make the bike more livable, like a seatpost wedge that actually works—an apparently high bar to clear in this day and age.

Settle in for a great episode of the Velo Podcast!

items.title: Giro d’Italia 2027 Route Reveal: Two Time Trials and Return of Zoncolan in Savage Final Week
items.author: ahood
items.content: Double Mortirolo, the Gavia, then the Zoncolan: The 2027 Giro delivers its biggest punches in brutal final week.
items.lbText:
Monte Zoncolan returns to the Giro d’Italia in 2027 as the final exclamation point in a punishing third week that also packs in legendary climbs with a double ascent of the Mortirolo.

Organizers unveiled a challenging old-school course of 3,418.9km and 50,250m of climbing between the May 8 start in Trieste and the May 30 finish in the Italian capital, Rome.

The 110th edition of the corsa rosa will test the overall contenders, with two individual time trials totaling 56.9km, trademark early summit finishes, and an endless barrage of mountains following the second rest day across the Dolomites.

Will the course be tempting enough to attract the likes of defending champion Jonas Vingegaard or perhaps French ace Paul Seixas ?

The headline act is the return to Monte Zoncolan — the OG of cycling’s “impossible climbs” — for the first time since 2021. Riders will climb up the Ovaro approach, where Chris Froome won in 2018, on the Giro’s penultimate stage.

Before that comes an explosive day through the Alps, with the Mortirolo appearing twice along with the Gavia in a stage packing 5,700m of climbing in the Giro’s epic “queen stage.”

There is room for the fast men, too. Organizers circled six stages as sprint opportunities, alongside eight hilly stages, five mountaintop finales, and the two time trials.

The Giro opens with nine consecutive racing days and enough climbing to separate the pink jersey pretenders from the contenders.

Trieste hosts an opening stage that crosses into Slovenia and squeezes three challenging climbs into the final 40km. Stage 2 stays entirely in Slovenia, linking Ljubljana and Koper, before another demanding day from Cervignano to Possagno.

Who knows? Maybe Tadej Pogačar will show up to race.

The sprinters should get their first clear opening at Misano’s motor racing circuit on stage 4.

The GC battle clicks into gear early with stage 5, starting in Filottrano to honor Michele Scarponi 10 years after his death. The day’s 139km pack 3,300 meters of climbing.

The first of two TTs comes with the 19.6km run from Sulmona to an uphill finish at Campo di Giove.

Naples follows before the opening Sunday brings another summit finish at Monte Livata.

The second week serves up plenty of asphalt to attack before the race reaches the brutal mountains looming in the north.

Racing resumes with 218km from Palombara Sabina to Norcia, where repeated climbs and descents totaling 3,600m sets the tone for week 2 packed with potential ambush country.

The race’s longest stage follows, finishing at the Mugello Circuit in a likely opportunity for the sprinters.

Tuscany then hosts the Tappa Bartali from Montecatini Terme to Zeri, featuring Passo dei Due Santi and a new uphill finish. A flatter run into Reggio Emilia offers some relief before a demanding weekend.

Saturday’s 187-kilometer stage to Piani di Bobbio/Valtorta gets heavy with 4,900m of climbing. The Ghisallo, Culmine di San Pietro, Miragolo San Salvatore, and Alino precede the uphill finale.

The week closes with the 37.3km individual time trial starts inside Monza’s racing circuit and finishes in Milan. The flat but technical route will favor the specialists and pressure the pure climbers to limit the losses.

The Giro comes out swinging for a brutal, old-school third week.

Coming a day after the rest day, stage 16 from Sondrio to Aprica could blow up the race at 192km and 5,700m of climbing. The stage features two ascents of the Mortirolo with the feared Gavia packed in between. The Gavia carries Cima Coppi honors as the Giro’s highest point, while the Mortirolo is the designated Montagna Pantani.

The sprinters get another chance from Chiari to Vo’ before the mountains return on the road from Rovereto to Madonna di Campiglio. Rovereto to Sacile, featuring 3,000m of climbing in 199km is perfect for the breakaways.

Then comes the return of Monte Zoncolan. The penultimate stage starts in Pordenone and finishes up the steeper Ovaro face in the final chance to crack the race wide open.

Rome is back for the final stage to pop the champagne after one last bunch kick.

items.title: Zwift Rider Spots ‘A Guy Taking a Dump’ in New Real-World Video Package
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Zwift rushes to remove images of a figure squatting in the roadside bushes from its new premium 'Plus' world after user post goes viral.
items.lbText:
One Zwift user got more than they were bargaining for when they took the platform’s new “real life” video format for a spin.

Sam Sky was virtually grinding along the Colorado River Sunrise highway on his indoor trainer when he spotted someone in the corner of his screen, crouched in bushes in the lay-by.

There was only one thing they could reasonably be doing: “Taking a dump.”

Sky grabbed a screencap of this surprise addition to Zwift’s new “Plus” package and shared it to the Zwift Ride Owners Group on Facebook.

“Zoom in on the green circle. I saw a guy taking a dump by the side of the road during my session this morning on the new videos,” Sky wrote Monday in the text accompanying his post.

And indeed, if you zoom in close enough, Sky doesn’t seem to be mistaken.

A figure with a white top can be seen hunched over, seemingly pushing their own take of Zone 2 into some scrubby foliage.

The post’s comments section inevitably lit up. Bad jokes about Tom Dumoulin mingled with snarky comments that Sky wasn’t training hard enough.

Zwift rolled out its “Plus” premium tier last week to a wave of hype.

The online training and racing giant added real-world video routes and adaptive coaching to a costly subscription model it considered a milestone.

For the first time, Zwifters could ascend iconic real-world climbs and zoom along touristic coastal roads rather than take on another rep of Watopia’s “Epic KoM.”

Excited early adopters like Sky likely didn’t expect Zwift’s expansion into the real world to be quite this realistic, however.

But fear not, Zwift is clearing up the mess.

A spokesperson told Road.CC on Tuesday that they’re working to scrub this unfortunate addition from its new premium package.

“We’re aware that the screenshot has been shared,” Zwift told Road.CC . “This is being addressed today. I’m sure that some readers may be slightly disappointed.”

You can check Velo editor Josh Ross’ deep-dive review of Zwift Plus here . No dumps included.

items.title: Giro d’Italia Women 2027 Route Reveal: Uphill Time Trial and Monte Bianco Finale
items.author: ahood
items.content: Something for everyone before a final Alpine showdown: The 2027 Giro d'Italia Women ends with a climbing time trial and a brutal Monte Bianco queen stage.
items.lbText:
There's plenty of climbing in the 2027 edition of Giro Women. (Photo: Getty Images/RCS Sport)

The 2027 Giro d’Italia Women starts by the beach, but anyone chasing pink better bring their climbing legs.

An uphill time trial, two summit finishes, and a final showdown in the shadow of Mont Blanc headline a nine-stage route unveiled in Rome that leaves the climbers plenty to chew on.

Defending champion Demi Vollering will have her hands full, if she decides to return next season .

Running May 29 to June 6, the race covers 1,132km and packs in 17,450m of climbing between the seaside start in Viareggio and the mountainous finale in the Aosta Valley.

That is plenty of vertical packed into nine days for the season’s first women’s grand tour after La Vuelta Femenina is moved to October.

The first major summit comes on stage 4, from Credaro to Passo della Presolana. Two days later, the Bergamo to Madesimo-Valle Spluga stage delivers another uphill finish that should help separate the pink jersey contenders.

Passo San Marco tops out at 1,987m to claim the Cima Alfonsina Strada as the race’s highest point.

The Valdigne Tudor uphill time trial is stacked up with the closing Monte Bianco stage in the final weekend to guarantee the race won’t be decided until the last summit.

The sprinters get three stages early on, with two hilly stages offering opportunities for attackers. Three mountain stages and the uphill time trial complete the menu.

items.title: EF Education-EasyPost Reinvents Itself as Cycling’s Super Teams Get Richer
items.author: ahood
items.content: Carapaz out. Wegelius gone. Matt White back. EF undergoes a radical makeover as Vaughters reshapes the WorldTour squad to take on the peloton's richest teams.
items.lbText:
EF Education-EasyPost has always managed to hit big results. (Photo: Gruber Images)

EF Education-EasyPost is heading into 2027 with a smaller budget, a radical roster makeover, and some big questions about how to stay competitive in the super team era.

Richard Carapaz is gone. Longtime sports director Charly Wegelius is out. Matt White is back. And team pink is loading up on unknown talent and betting on aging stars.

The team’s DNA remains the money ball underdog in cycling’s super team era.

“I see us as a team of opportunity,” said Jonathan Vaughters , founder and CEO of EF Pro Cycling. “For young riders, we want to be the team that gives them their first real chance to excel at the WorldTour level. For others, we want to offer a second chance. Tao Geoghegan Hart is a great example of that.”

The financial arms race in the WorldTour isn’t slowing down, so EF is adapting.

UAE Emirates-XRG, Visma-Lease a Bike, Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, and Lidl-Trek continue to stack their rosters with expensive stars and emerging talent.

Vaughters knows EF — which packs a middle-of-the-peloton budget — cannot win a bidding war against cycling’s deepest pockets.

The challenge is finding riders the super teams overlook and try to develop young talent before their price tags explode, and then deliver results when and where the argyle army can.

“But more than anything, I want every rider on this team to have an opportunity to shine. We’re not going to build our entire racing strategy around protecting individual leaders,” he said. “We want to race openly and give everyone the freedom to take their chances.”

It’s the latest shape-shifting for a team that has long punched above its financial weight against the sport’s richest teams.

The long-running U.S. team — dating back to 2007 — has never had the biggest budget in the peloton, and now it’s facing its latest challenge to remain competitive just as deep-pocketed teams keep piling on .

Carapaz still had another year on his contract, but EF agreed to release him early .

“We willingly let Richie go. It was not forced,” Vaughters told the Escape Collective . “We needed to make some hard decisions … A very simple option would be to just let your most highly compensated rider leave.”

Carapaz is not the only big-name departure as the team tries to find a space to remain competitive without blowing out the bank.

Georg Steinhauser, one of the team’s most promising young climbers, is heading to Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe.

Classics specialists Kasper Asgreen and Michael Valgren are also leaving, along with Madis Mihkels, Mikkel Honoré, James Shaw, and rising Spanish talent Markel Beloki.

The departures of some of the team’s most prolific performers means the team will have to reshuffle its racing style for next season.

“We’re going to be opportunistic, to see possibilities that other teams might miss. We’ve always raced that way, but in 2027, we’re going to take it even further,” Vaughters said. “I think that’s something really unique in the WorldTour.”

Vaughters is hoping to find space between the bidding wars at the top to carve out some wins by racing against the odds.

The upheaval isn’t limited to the roster.

Wegelius, one of EF’s most influential sports directors, is leaving after 15 seasons with the organization.

The Briton joined the former Garmin setup in 2012 and his departure follows other changes in the management structure, including the exits of Tejay Van Garderen and Matti Breschel.

Coming in is Australian veteran Matt White , who returns to the team where he launched his sports director career in 2008 after stints at Jayco-AlUla and Movistar.

White joins an established group of sports directors, including Juanma Gárate, Carmen Small, Tom Southam, Daniel Foder, Andreas Klier, Michael Creed, Huub Duijn, Ken Vanmarcke, and Sebastian Langeveld. Recently retired Dan McLay also joins as a sport director.

“I genuinely believe we have the best group of people working behind the scenes of any team in the WorldTour,” Vaughters said. “Our goal is to connect all of those dots, from the moment we first identify a promising young rider to the moment they’re competing for victories at the biggest races in the world. That’s how we build a team that can win today and continue getting better in the years ahead.”

White and the other sport directors will have pressure to deliver results right out of the gate.

The team will have one eye on the UCI team rankings. Coming out of 2026 in the first season of a three-year WorldTour cycle, EF was ranked 15th among teams chasing points to secure its next WorldTour license at the end of 2028.

With a spending war playing out across the peloton, Vaughters and EF’s brain trust have targeted riders with something to prove.

Former Giro d’Italia champion Geoghegan Hart arrives from Lidl-Trek while Colombian climber Iván Sosa returns to the WorldTour.

German prospect Emil Herzog joins from Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe on a deal through 2029 and Tobias Bayer brings classics experience from Alpecin, while young American Gavin Sherry is among several riders stepping up from the team’s development program.

“We have a really exciting opportunity to build something special with the young talent coming through our program,” Vaughters said. “EF Education-Aevolo is a big part of that, but it’s also about the riders and staff we already have at the WorldTour level. We’ve had the youngest team in the WorldTour for a few years now, and we intend to continue that.”

It’s a calculated gamble on two fronts. Riders like Herzog and Sherry represent EF’s future, while Geoghegan Hart and Sosa see a chance to revive stalled careers.

If even one or two deliver, EF could find some serious payback in a transfer market dominated by bigger spenders.

Ben Healy and Neilson Powless remain as the men’s team’s most important anchors heading into 2027.…
